name: Hebrew Bible
info: The Hebrew Bible is the canonical collection of Hebrew scriptures, the Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, composed and edited by the Israelites over several hundred years; its authoritative Jewish form was fixed in the Masoretic Text of the 7th to 10th centuries CE.

facts.made: The Israelites, in Samaria and Judah and later in exile and the Second Temple period; tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses, at least 73 psalms to David and three books to Solomon, while scholars see composition and editing in stages
facts.form: Twenty-four books in three divisions (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim), mostly in Biblical Hebrew with a few passages in Biblical Aramaic; prose, poetry, law, prophecy and wisdom writing
facts.where: Read in Jewish and Christian worship and study worldwide; the Aleppo Codex and the Leningrad Codex are Tiberian Masoretic manuscripts; other witnesses include the Septuagint, the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Dead Sea Scrolls
facts.known: The Torah and the Law of Moses; the covenant between God and Israel; monotheism; the Psalms; wisdom books such as Proverbs and Ecclesiastes; the prophets; the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint translation

t: Jewish tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses, while most scholars see the books as composed and edited in stages over several hundred years, receiving their final shape in the Second Temple period.
Its three parts, the Torah, the Nevi'im and the Ketuvim, reached canonical status one after another, and scholars disagree on when the canon was fixed.
The Masoretic Text of the 7th to 10th centuries CE is the form authoritative in Judaism today, and it differs in places from older witnesses such as the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
dyk: The Hebrew Bible has 8,679 distinct words, of which 1,480 occur only once. The count of 24 books is somewhat arbitrary, since the twelve Minor Prophets are counted as a single book.
ev: Scholars estimate that the Jacob tradition of Genesis 25–35 was first written down in the north, probably at the sanctuary of Bethel
The northern Kingdom of Samaria is conquered by the Neo-Assyrian Empire
The Kingdom of Judah is conquered by the Neo-Babylonian Empire, the Temple is destroyed and many Judaeans are exiled to Babylon
Cyrus the Great of Persia conquers Babylon and grants the Judaean exiles freedom to return to Zion
The Book of Daniel is written, and is not grouped with the Prophets, presumably because that collection was already fixed
Some scholars place the completion of the canon here, while others date it earlier; rabbis between 70 and 100 CE had debated which books make the hands unclean
The compilation of the Masoretic Text by Jewish scribes and scholars begins, a work of the 7th to 10th centuries CE that added vowel markings to the text
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its Tanakh, replacing its translation of 1917

sections.origins:
The Hebrew Bible was created by the Israelites, a people who lived within the cultural and religious context of the ancient Near East. Modern scholars such as Israel Finkelstein believe that the ancient Israelites mostly originated within Canaan: their material culture was closely related to that of their Canaanite neighbours, and Hebrew was a Canaanite dialect. Archaeological evidence indicates that Israel began as loosely organised tribal villages in the hill country c. 1250 – c. 1000 BCE.

By the 9th or 8th centuries BCE the scribal culture of Samaria and Judah was developed enough to produce biblical texts. The Kingdom of Samaria was more powerful and culturally advanced than Judah, and it had several cultic sites, among them the sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan. Some material may be older still. It is thought highly likely that extensive oral transmission of proverbs, stories and songs took place, and the Song of Deborah in Judges 5, with its archaic Hebrew, may reflect older oral traditions. Some stories also show contact with the literature of neighbouring peoples: Andrew R. George points to the similarity between the Genesis flood narrative and the Gilgamesh flood myth.
sections.content:
The Tanakh, also called the Hebrew Bible or Mikra, has three divisions. The Torah ('Teaching' or 'Instruction') holds Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, the foundational narrative of the Israelites and the Law of Moses. The Nevi'im ('Prophets') run from the Israelites' entry into the land to the Babylonian captivity of Judah. The Ketuvim ('Writings') include the Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five scrolls and the books of Daniel, Ezra–Nehemiah and Chronicles. The name Tanakh is an acronym of the three Hebrew names.

The narrative begins with creation and the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whose children become the ancestors of the Twelve Tribes. It follows the Israelites in Egypt, the Exodus, forty years in the wilderness, the entry into Canaan, the judges, and the monarchy of Saul, David and Solomon. It then tells of the division into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the southern Kingdom of Judah, and of the exile and return.

A central theme is monotheism. John Barton writes that YHWH is presented as the God who created the world and the only God with whom Israel is to be concerned. The relationship is described as a covenant, and the text sets ethical requirements, including justice for widows, orphans and other vulnerable groups. Genres include law, history, hymns, wisdom literature, prophecy and apocalyptic writing.
sections.making:
Religious tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses, and later biblical texts call it the Torah of Moses. The Torah itself credits Moses with writing only some specific sections. Tradition credits David with at least 73 of the Psalms and Solomon with Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Solomon. Scholars date the Torah to the 1st millennium BCE, after Israel and Judah had developed as states. John J. Collins writes that all the Hebrew Bible received its final shape in the postexilic, or Second Temple, period.

Scholars reconstruct a gradual process. The Jacob tradition was probably first written down in the north in the 8th century BCE. The Moses and Exodus story also appears to be northern, and existed as a self-contained story before it was joined to the patriarchal stories during or after the exile; the account of Moses's birth resembles that of Sargon of Akkad, which suggests Neo-Assyrian influence after 722 BCE. The Book of Judges was written c. 600 BCE, around 500 years after the events it describes. The author of the Books of Kings likely lived in Jerusalem. E. Theodore Mullen argued that the Deuteronomistic History was composed during the Babylonian captivity, and that the Tetrateuch was compiled in the Persian era. The Book of Daniel was written c. 164 BCE.
sections.reception:
The three divisions gained authority one after another. The Torah achieved canonical status first, possibly as early as the 5th century BCE, as Ezra 7:6 suggests. The Nevi'im had canonical status by the 2nd century BCE, since the Book of Sirach, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the New Testament refer to the Law and the Prophets. The Ketuvim came last, and its content seems to have stayed fluid until the process was completed in the 2nd century CE. There is no scholarly consensus on when the canon was fixed: some argue for the Hasmonean dynasty, others for the 2nd century CE or later. The Council of Jamnia, once credited with fixing it, is not believed by modern scholars to have been an authoritative council. According to the Talmud, much of the Tanakh was compiled by the men of the Great Assembly, a task completed in 450 BCE.

Scholars have also stressed its part in Jewish identity. Fergus Millar called it both a national history and a source of law, and biblical laws such as circumcision, Shabbat observance and dietary prohibitions became markers of Jewish identity. Within Judaism, the classical approach to commentary assumes divine inspiration, with Rashi the major commentary on the Chumash. The Orthodox community considers the study of the Bible as a human creation heresy when applied to the Torah, while Non-Orthodox Jews accept both approaches.
sections.survival:
Centuries of hand-copying produced textual variants. Scribes introduced thousands of minor changes, sometimes by accident and sometimes to add clarifications or theological material. Ancient Hebrew was written without vowels. In the early Middle Ages the Masoretes created a single system of vocalisation, chiefly Aaron ben Moses ben Asher in the Tiberias school, based on the oral tradition for reading the Tanakh, hence the name Tiberian vocalisation. Some traditional sources and some Orthodox Jews hold that the pronunciation and cantillation derive from the revelation at Sinai. The resulting Masoretic Text, of the 7th to 10th centuries CE, became the authoritative version, and the Aleppo Codex and the Leningrad Codex are Tiberian Masoretic codices.

Other witnesses survive. They are the Septuagint, the Syriac Peshitta, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Targum Onkelos and quotations in rabbinic manuscripts. These may be older than the Masoretic Text in some cases and often differ from it, and this has given rise to the theory of an Urtext. Such a text has never been found, and which of the Septuagint, the Masoretic Text and the Samaritan Pentateuch is closest to it is debated. The Samaritans produced their own version of the Torah, and Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria produced the Septuagint.
sections.legacy:
For Jews the Hebrew Bible is the scripture of their religion and, scholars argue, a foundation of their identity. David Goodblatt argued that it underpinned Jewish nationalism in the Second Temple period, and Adrian Hastings held that the study of sacred texts helped the Jews preserve national identity after the loss of their political entity in the 1st century CE. The Bible also helped preserve Hebrew, which, unlike Phoenician and Edomite, survived even as Aramaic replaced other regional languages. The five scrolls are read aloud in many synagogues on set occasions: the Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth at Shavuot, Lamentations on Tisha B'Av, Ecclesiastes at Sukkot and Esther at Purim.

Christianity has long asserted a close relationship between the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, and its books are included in the Old Testament of the Christian Bible. The Septuagint was influential on early Christianity, and the translations used by Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches are based on it. In Islam, the Tawrat is often identified with the Pentateuch and also with the other books of the Hebrew Bible. Hastings contended that the model of ancient Israel in the Hebrew Bible set the original concept of nationhood. Scholars have also questioned the historicity of the patriarchs, the Exodus and the conquest, though Avraham Faust notes that some traditions align with archaeology from the 9th century BCE onward.

summary: The Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh, is the canonical collection of Hebrew scriptures in three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim. Tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses; scholars see composition in stages, with the Masoretic Text authoritative in Judaism.

Article says the Torah achieved canonical status 'possibly as early as the 5th century BCE'; kept hedged.
Left out: Hayes's 'religious and cultural revolution' quotation, the Iliad/Odyssey 24-book speculation, the 22-book and Athanasius counts, the list of modern translations beyond the 1985 JPS Tanakh.
